Pratikramana (Sanskrit: प्रतिक्रमण, romanized: Pratikramaṇa; also spelled Pratikraman) (lit. "introspection"), is a ritual during which Jains repent (prayaschit) for their sins and non-meritorious activities committed knowingly or inadvertently during their daily life through thought, speech or action.
Pratikramana also refers to a combition of six avashyaks (essential rituals), being Samayik (state of total equanimity), Chauvisantho (honoring the 24 Tirthankars), Vandana – (offering salutations to sadhus (monks) and sadhvis (nuns)), Pratikramana (introspection and repentance), Kayotsarga (meditation of the soul) and Pratyakhyan (renunciation).
Although frequency of repenting varies, devout Jains often practice Pratikraman at least twice a day. It is one of the 28 primary attributes (mūla guņa) of both Śvētāmbara and Digambara monks.
Pratikramana is the combination of two words, Pra meaning "return" and atikramana meaning "violation". Literally, it means "returning from violations".[1]
There are five types of Pratikramana:
- Devasi
- Ray
- Pakhi
- Chaumasi
- Samvatsari
Devasi Pratikramana' is performed daily in the evening.
Rayi Pratikraman is performed in the early morning.
Pakhi Pratikramana is done once every fifteen days. It falls on 15th and 30th dates (sud and vad) of the Hindu calendar month.
Chaumasi Pratikramana is done once in four months on the Purnima (full moon) of the Kartik, Falgun and Aṣaṛh months of the Vira Nirvana Samvat calendrical year for the sins committed during that period.
Samvatsari Pratikraman is done once per year on the last day of Paryushana mahaparv for the sins committed during the whole year. As per holy Jain Agamas, Samvatsari Pratikaman is practiced on the 4th/5th day (sud) of Bhadarva month of the Hindu calendar.
Samvatsari Pratikraman includes all six things a Śrāvaka (householders) must do.[2]
Jainism considers the soul, in its pure form, to have infinite perception, knowledge, and vigor, and to be non-attached. These attributes are not seen in a worldly soul because it is soiled with karmas. By following religious principles and activities, Jains believe they overcome karmas and promote liberation of the soul. There are various rituals, of which Pratikraman is the most important. During pratikraman, Jains repent for non-meritorious activities on a daily basis.[3]
Pratikraman must be performed twice every day, or at least once every day after sunset. If that is not possible, at least on every Pakkhi (24 times in a year). If that is not possible, at least one every Chaumasi (3 times in a year). If none of the above is possible a Jain must perform at least Samvatsari Pratikraman (once a year).[4]
Pratikramana is also done while performing the sāmāyika (periodic concentration). In performing sāmāyika, the śrāvaka has to stand and follow a procedure to begin a sāmāyika. Later, 48 minutes after beginning a sāmāyika, the śrāvaka ends the sāmāyika with a procedure.[5][6]
Chauvisantho, also called Chaturvinshatistava, means adoration of the twenty-four Tirthankaras. While reciting it, Jains show their respect for the Tirthankaras and are reminded of how victorious these Jinas were, who overcame inner enemies like anger, ego, greed, deceit, etc. Chauvisantho encourages Jains to emulate Tirthankars and strive to be like them.

SOURCE jaingpt.com (Pratikraman: Meaning and the Six Avashyakas | JainGPT):
Pratikraman
'Turning back' - the structured self-review at the centre of Jain practice, performed daily by some and once a year by many.
Pratikraman means "to turn back" — to return from where one has strayed to where one undertook to stand. It is the central rite of Jain practice: a structured review of one's own conduct over a defined period, followed by confession, repentance, and a resolution against repetition.
Most Jains encounter it once a year, as Samvatsari Pratikraman on the last day of Paryushan. Ascetics perform it twice every day.
What it is for
Jain doctrine holds that karma is matter that adheres to the soul through action, speech and thought, and that it can be shed. Pratikraman is one of the means of shedding it. The reasoning is precise: karma bound through carelessness is loosened by attention, and karma bound through a fault repeated without noticing is loosened by noticing.
This is why the rite is so specific and so long. A general admission of imperfection changes nothing. The liturgy walks through the vows one by one and names the particular ways each may have been violated — which forces the practitioner to check each against their actual conduct rather than skip to a comfortable summary.
The six avashyakas
Pratikraman is built from six obligatory practices, the shad-avashyaka. Performed in order, they take the practitioner from settling the mind to committing to the period ahead.
| # | Avashyaka | What it is | 
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Samayika | Establishing equanimity. A fixed period — classically 48 minutes — of sitting in a state of even-mindedness, renouncing harmful activity for its duration. Everything after this happens inside that state. | 
| 2 | Chaturvimshati-stava | Praise of the twenty-four Tirthankaras, recited as the Logassa. Not petition: the Tirthankaras are liberated and grant nothing. It is the holding up of a standard against which conduct is about to be measured. | 
| 3 | Vandana | Veneration of one's teacher and of ascetics, with a formal request for permission and pardon. | 
| 4 | Pratikramana | Repentance proper — the itemised review of faults against the vows over the period. | 
| 5 | Kayotsarga | Literally "abandonment of the body": standing or sitting motionless, attention withdrawn from the body, for a counted number of breaths. The stillness in which what was just reviewed is absorbed. | 
| 6 | Pratyakhyana | Renunciation — taking a vow for the period ahead. The rite does not end in regret; it ends in a specific undertaking. | 
The five kinds
Pratikraman is named for the period it reviews. The longer the interval, the longer and more thorough the rite.
- Devasi — performed in the evening, reviewing the day just passed.
- Rai — performed at dawn, reviewing the night.
- Pakkhi — fortnightly, on the fourteenth day of each lunar fortnight.
- Chaumasi — every four months, at the turn of each season.
- Samvatsari — annual, on the last day of Paryushan. This is the minimum: a Jain who performs pratikraman only once in the year performs this one.
Samvatsari Pratikraman
The annual form runs for several hours, typically beginning in the afternoon and continuing into the evening, and it is the one occasion when the hall is full. It covers the whole year, and it is exhaustive by design — transgressions against each of the twelve vows of a householder, against right faith and right knowledge, against the restraint of the senses, and against the five classes of one-sensed beings.

Understanding Pratikraman
Pratikraman is one of the most essential rituals in Jain practice — a structured process of introspection, confession, and repentance that every Jain is encouraged to perform. The word itself reveals its purpose: "Pra" means return, and "atikraman" means transgression or deviation. Thus, Pratikraman literally means "returning from transgressions" — a systematic turning back from wrong actions to the right path.
In Jain philosophy, even the most mindful person commits transgressions in daily life — harming tiny organisms while walking, speaking harshly, harboring jealousy, or indulging in excess. These actions bind new karma to the soul. Pratikraman is the prescribed remedy: by sincerely acknowledging these errors, asking forgiveness, and resolving not to repeat them, the practitioner loosens the grip of newly bound karma.
There are several types of Pratikraman based on frequency. Pratikraman is ideally performed twice daily — Devasi Pratikraman in the evening (reflecting on the day's transgressions) and Rai Pratikraman in the morning (reflecting on the previous night's transgressions). Pakkhik Pratikraman is performed fortnightly. Chaumasi Pratikraman is performed every four months. And the most widely observed is Samvatsari Pratikraman, performed annually during Paryushana, when Jains seek forgiveness from all living beings.
The Samvatsari Pratikraman is considered so important that even those who cannot perform daily Pratikraman make every effort to attend this annual observance. It culminates in the universal declaration: "Micchami Dukkadam" — "May my improper actions be forgiven."
The Six Essential Components (Avashyak)
Pratikraman is part of a larger framework of six essential daily duties (Shad Avashyak) prescribed for every Jain. Understanding these components helps appreciate how Pratikraman fits into the broader spiritual practice:
1. Samayik — Attaining equanimity through 48-minute meditation
2. Chaturvimshati Stava — Praising the 24 Tirthankaras through hymns and devotion
3. Vandana — Paying respect to the Guru (spiritual teacher)
4. Pratikraman — Confessing and repenting for transgressions
5. Kayotsarga — Meditation through body abandonment (standing perfectly still)
6. Pratyakhyana — Taking vows of future restraint
During the actual Pratikraman ritual, all six of these elements are woven together into a cohesive practice. The ritual moves through phases of recitation, confession, meditation, and resolution, creating a complete spiritual exercise.
Step-by-Step Guide to Performing Pratikraman
While detailed Pratikraman procedures vary between Shvetambar and Digambar traditions and specific sub-sects, the following outlines the general flow of a Devasi (evening) Pratikraman as practiced in the Shvetambar tradition:
Preparation: Wear clean clothes, go to the upashray or temple, or find a clean space at home. Apply muhpatti and sit on a clean mat facing north or east.
Opening: Begin with the Navkar Mantra (recited three times). This establishes devotion and centers the mind.

Tassa Uttari Sutra: A further confession seeking to cover any transgressions that the Iriyavahiyam may not have addressed.
